content: SOAP (Simple Object Access Protocol) is a protocol designed for the exchange of XML-based messages over computer networks, typically utilizing HTTP or HTTPS as the transport mechanism. It serves as the foundational layer of the web services protocol stack, providing a basic messaging framework upon which additional abstract layers can be constructed. For example, SOAP can be used to send a properly formatted request to a web service-enabled website, such as a real estate database, specifying the data ranges required for a search. The website would then respond with a structured XML document containing the requested results, including associated data such as property prices, locations, and features. This data can subsequently be integrated directly into a third-party application or website. SOAP supports various messaging patterns, but the most commonly employed is the Remote Procedure Call (RPC) pattern. In this pattern, a client node sends a request message to a server node, and the server immediately responds with a corresponding message. SOAP is considered the successor to XML-RPC, borrowing its transport and interaction neutrality as well as its envelope/header/body structure, likely influenced by WDDX. The SOAP specification was initially developed in 1998 by Dave Winer, Don Box, Bob Atkinson, and Mohsen Al-Ghosein, with support from Microsoft. It was originally conceived as an object-access protocol. The specification is now maintained by the XML Protocol Working Group of the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C). SOAP 1.2 became a W3C Recommendation on June 24, 2003. It is important to note that SOAP is distinct from SOA (Service-Oriented Architecture), despite occasional confusion between the two. Transport Methods SOAP utilizes an Internet application layer protocol as its transport mechanism. While some critics argue that this constitutes misuse of such protocols, proponents draw parallels to successful tunneling of other protocols at various levels. Both SMTP and HTTP are valid application layer protocols used for SOAP transport, though HTTP has gained broader acceptance due to its compatibility with modern Internet infrastructure, particularly network firewalls. This compatibility provides a significant advantage over distributed protocols like GIOP/IIOP or DCOM, which are often blocked by firewalls. XML was chosen as the standard message format for SOAP due to its widespread adoption by major corporations and open-source development communities. However, the verbose nature of XML can be both an advantage and a drawback. While it enhances human readability, it can slow down processing and become cumbersome. In contrast, other middleware technologies like CORBA, GIOP, ICE, and DCOM use more compact binary message formats. To address performance concerns, hardware appliances are available to accelerate XML message processing, and binary XML is being explored as a means to streamline throughput requirements. Technical Critique Numerous experts have analyzed the technical strengths and weaknesses of SOAP in comparison to alternative technologies and within the context of its intended use. Advantages: 1. SOAP facilitates easier communication through proxies and firewalls compared to earlier remote execution technologies. 2. It is versatile, supporting various transport protocols such as SMTP and RSS. 3. SOAP is platform-independent, allowing it to function across different operating systems. 4. It is language-independent, enabling interoperability between applications written in different programming languages. 5. SOAP is simple and extensible, making it adaptable to a wide range of use cases. Disadvantages: 1. The verbose XML format can make SOAP significantly slower than competing middleware technologies like CORBA, particularly when large messages are involved. However, this may not be an issue for small message exchanges. To improve performance for XML with embedded binary objects, mechanisms like Message Transmission Optimization Mechanism (MTOM) and VTD-XML have been introduced. 2. When relying on HTTP as the transport protocol without using WS-Addressing or an Enterprise Service Bus (ESB), the roles of interacting parties are fixed. Only the client can utilize the services of the server, necessitating polling instead of notification in many cases. 3. Many implementations of HTTP as a transport protocol for SOAP are done without consideration of how the operation would be modeled in HTTP. This design choice, while intentional, can lead to suboptimal results. For instance, a POST-based binding might be used for an operation that would be more naturally modeled as a GET operation in HTTP. This lack of alignment complicates proper analysis of the operation at the application-protocol level.
